text: State of the City Address Mayor Raj Salwan City of Fremont June 30, 2026 Welcome everyone. Good evening. I'd like to call this Special Council meeting to order, for the State of the City. <knock the gavel> <Mayor leads the Pledge of Allegiance> Now I'd like to welcome Angela Tirado to the stage to sing our National Anthem. I’m pleased she’s joining us again for this year’s State of the City Address. <Angela Tirado on stage to sing the National Anthem> Thank you for joining us for the 2026 State of the City Address. We're also Livestreaming this event online and on Channel 27, our Government Channel. Once again, good evening, Fremont. Thank you for being here and for the energy in this room. Seventy years ago this year, the people of Centerville, Mission San José, Niles, Irvington, and Warm Springs decided to do something bold. They decided to become one city. Five towns. Five identities. One shared bet — that we would be stronger together than we ever were apart. Seventy years later, we're still fulfilling that promise. That is Fremont. And this is your City Council. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont I'm honored to serve with my colleagues: Vice Mayor Yajing Zhang Councilmembers: Teresa Keng Desrie Campbell Kathy Kimberlin Yang Shao Raymond Liu I would like to thank the City Manager, Karena Shackelford, City Attorney, Rafael Alvarado, Jr. and the entire City Staff and Leadership team, For their contributions in making Fremont a desirable city to live, work, and play. Tonight I want to do two things. I want to look back at one of the most consequential years in this city’s history — and I want to look forward to what we build next. This is my second year as your Mayor. In my first year, we built relationships, set priorities, and strengthened our foundation with the determination of our incredible City staff. This year, that hard work began turning into visible results. We're not finding our footing anymore; we're building momentum. Year one was about listening, learning, and building trust. Year two is about execution — taking the priorities residents care about and turning them into action. And I'll tell you: building is the better job. Year one, I also spent a lot of time learning about the region, sitting down with fellow mayors and getting to know our County Supervisors, state legislators, Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont federal delegation, and regional partners. Building this kind of trust takes time, and the fruits of this labor show up later in rooms where Fremont needs a voice. Year two, these relationships are paying off. Of course, there were — and will continue to be — hard days. There always are. But I can tell you that I've never been more certain this city is on the right path. And it's worth remembering how far we’ve come. Seventy years ago, Fremont was orchards, farmland, and five small towns that much of the Bay Area barely knew. Today, we're the fourth largest city in the Bay Area, a global center of advanced manufacturing, and one of the most diverse cities in the entire country — where more than 100 languages are spoken in our schools. Nobody handed us that. We built it. One decision, one neighbor, one generation at a time. If there's one thing I want every resident watching tonight to take away, it's this: Fremont's hit its stride. There was one moment for me that made the whole year make sense. A few weeks ago, I was at Street Eats — our Downtown food-truck night — right here at the Downtown Event Center and Plaza. The sun was setting. The music was going. Families were walking through Downtown. Kids were running around with sticky popsicle hands. I spoke with a longtime Fremont resident named Kathy. She's called Fremont home for more than 50 years. She raised her kids in this city and helped run a small business in Niles. We got to talking about how fast Fremont's changing — Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont the new manufacturing companies, the small businesses lighting up Downtown, the energy you can feel walking down Capitol Avenue on a Friday night. And what she told me captured the whole challenge of this moment. She said she's excited to see Fremont responding to residents’ needs and creating quality jobs in advanced manufacturing. But what mattered most to her was simple: she wanted to know her grandkids could get jobs here and afford to stay in the place her family helped build. Then she said something that stayed with me: “We are no longer a bedroom community.” We are no longer a bedroom community. That came from a resident who's watched Fremont change for more than half a century. That, right there's, the whole job. Fremont has quietly become the place where America builds the future. And my job — our job — is to make sure that future is something every resident, every family, and every one of Kathy’s grandkids and yours can feel at home in. That's the story of this year. And that's the story I want to tell you tonight. So, let’s start with the boom. Because what's happening in Fremont right now is not normal. In 2025, 70% of all manufacturing leases in this region landed right here in Fremont. 70%. We're home to 33 AI server manufacturing facilities, four million square feet of them. Seven of the world’s 10 largest AI server makers are building servers here in Fremont, California. That's three times more than just two years ago. And we led all of Silicon Valley with five million square feet leased in 2025 across office, industrial, and R&D. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont We did not have those numbers two years ago. We did not have them last year. We have them now. Now, why should you care about square footage and lease numbers? Because every one of those buildings represents jobs. Paychecks. Opportunity. Families who can live and work here. And every one of those companies contributes to the tax base that funds the police officers, firefighters, parks, roads, services, and programs I'm going to talk about tonight. When Fremont wins these companies, Fremont residents win. That's the connection I never want you to lose sight of. Let me put some names on it. Physical Intelligence and Agility — two of the most-watched robotics companies in the country — chose Fremont. Bloom Energy expanded its fuel-cell operation right here. Tesla deepened its footprint, and so did Lam Research. We are building the batteries and materials of the future with companies like Stacked Energy and Kuprion while also crafting the flying taxis and mobility systems for the next decade with Wisk Aero. We're advancing life sciences with Boehringer Ingelheim, Bionova Scientific, and Novo Nordisk. And we're home to the AI hardware leaders racing to build the backbone of the entire artificial-intelligence economy — Quanta, Hyve, Wistron, Mitac, AMAX, Aivres, and more. If you want to know where America's building its future, you walk into a building here in Fremont. This isn’t just meaningful locally; Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont it’s meaningful for our country. For a generation, America has sent too much manufacturing overseas. Factories closed. Skills left. Supply chains became fragile. Right now, America's trying to bring back the capacity to build the most advanced things in the world. The question is... where. Increasingly, the answer is, here. Fremont's one of the places where America's relearning how to build the future. That's economic history happening in real time — and Fremont leading it. Now, none of this happens by accident, and none of it happens without power. This year, we secured more than one billion dollars in expanded utility infrastructure. We doubled the capacity of our entire electrical grid compared to 2023: • 105 megawatts from PG&E • Nearly 200 megawatts of new microgrids, • Which includes 100 megawatts from Fremont based Bloom Energy. Likewise, the LS Power “Power the South Bay” Initiative — a half-billion-dollar investment — will add major transmission capacity and include conduit for future municipal broadband running underneath it. I want to be candid about why these investments matter. All over this country, cities are losing companies — not because they don't want them, but because they can't power them. The single biggest constraint on advanced manufacturing today is electricity. We saw that wall coming, Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont and we built around it before we hit it. That's the difference between a city that reacts, and a city that leads. But here's what I want every parent watching tonight to know. These jobs, these factories, these companies — they're not just for people from somewhere else. They're for your kids. The 14th annual Fremont Manufacturing Week was the largest in the country, with 17 participating companies and nearly 500 students from K-12 through college exploring semiconductors, biotech, robotics, autotech, clean tech, and advanced manufacturing. At the Engineering Expo, I watched FUSD and Mission Valley ROP students showcase projects that would've stunned me at twice their age. Ohlone College’s Earn-and-Learn program and Manufacturing Development Program are creating paid, on-the-job pathways into real careers. The Semiconductor Skills Bridge Academy is preparing students for one of the most important industries of the next generation. San Francisco Bay University’s inaugural Fremont Tech Week brought founders, students, employers, and innovators together right here in our city. Here's the pipeline I want for every kid in Fremont: you start in an FUSD classroom. You build something with your hands at the Engineering Expo. You earn a credential at Ohlone or MVROP. And you walk into a real, good-paying career without ever having to leave the city you grew up in. That's not a dream. We're building the rungs of that ladder right now. And we deepened our partnership with our schools to do it, because a great city and great schools rise together. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont The students in an FUSD classroom today are the engineers, nurses, teachers, entrepreneurs, technicians, and council members of Fremont 2050. By design, this boom's being built for the next generation of Fremont. And it's not only the large industrial campuses. Our Downtown is filling in with new housing rising above new ground-floor shops, new restaurants, and new reasons to come Downtown on a Friday night instead of driving somewhere else. These businesses looked across the Bay Area and chose Downtown Fremont. There were nearly 300 events and rentals by the City, organizations, private groups, and others held at this very building— the Downtown Event Center — drawing tens of thousands of people into the heart of our city. We're not just growing. We're building a Downtown with a heart. And this year’s Fremont Restaurant Week showed exactly what that can look like. Seventy restaurants participated, and 91% reported increased foot traffic or revenue. More than 113,000 total visits were recorded among participating restaurants. That's not just a food event. That's economic development, culture, and community pride tied into one. It’s Fremont showing the Bay Area who we are. The event even featured Fremont’s newest resident, who’s here with us tonight— DoorDash Dot, the autonomous delivery robot — which generated buzz among food influencers and brought national media attention to our city. In Fremont, small businesses, Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont food culture, advanced manufacturing, technology, and innovation are not separate stories. They're connected. That's the Fremont story. Now, I know what some of you're thinking right now. That all sounds great, Mayor. The cranes. The companies. The billion-dollar grid. The AI hardware. The lease numbers. But what does any of that mean for me? This year, we asked you that question directly. The 2025 resident satisfaction survey reached 636 residents in three languages. You told us two things very clearly. One: you're worried about cost of living. And two: you're worried about how we respond to encampments. I hear you. So tonight, I want to talk about how growth pays for the things residents actually care about. Let’s start with housing. We promised you five new affordable housing properties in 2025. We delivered all five. 567 new affordable units — open and serving Fremont families. Over half of the units at Bell Street Gardens are now leased by families who were homeless or at risk of homelessness. These families now have a stable place to live. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont We permitted 177 new accessory dwelling units, or ADUs last year — a 33% increase from the year before. And we launched a new program that provides homeowners with a pathway to legalize qualifying unpermitted ADUs already on their property. There're 769 more affordable units in the pipeline across six brand-new developments. And in this coming fiscal year, our First-Time Homebuyer Program will deliver approximately 10 brand-new, belowmarket-price homes for Fremont families. Is it enough? No. It's never enough when families are struggling. But the direction's clear. And we're not slowing down. Behind those numbers is a strategy. We've a state-certified Housing Element, which means Fremont has a real, approved plan to build homes at every income level. We zoned for more housing near transit, are supporting affordable housing, and we're cutting the red tape that makes building slow and expensive. Housing's not just about units. It's about whether teachers, firefighters, police officers, nurses, seniors, young families, and adult children can stay in the community they love. Now for that second concern: homelessness. This is where I want to be direct with you. We're making real progress, and we're not finished. Our approach is compassionate, but it's not passive. We offer services, shelter, outreach, behavioral health support, rental assistance, and housing navigation. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont But we also have a responsibility to keep parks, creeks, sidewalks, neighborhoods, and public spaces safe, clean, and accessible for everyone. The goal's not to move people from one street to another. It’s to move people toward stability, while restoring public spaces for the entire community. This year, our Winter Relief program opened a month early with 25% more capacity than last year. We signed a new two-year agreement with Bay Area Community Services to operate our Housing Navigation Center, which has helped 293 individuals since opening in 2020, of which 60% exited the program into stable housing. At Isherwood Park, we led a multi-department cleanup and outreach effort, during which 80% of those affected accepted relocation services. That's the number I want you to remember. 80% accepted help. We also removed approximately 800 cubic yards of debris — which is equivalent to roughly 60 dump trucks — from the site. That work required coordination with Union City, East Bay Regional Park District, Alameda County Water District, outreach providers, public safety teams, and environmental response crews. It was difficult work. And I want to extend my sincere gratitude to everyone who made it possible. You showed us what a coordinated response can do: outreach, services, shelter, environmental cleanup, public safety, and accountability working together. Back to our broader efforts, Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont we expanded our partnership with Alameda County Behavioral Health and resumed crisis services to supplement MET, our Mobile Evaluation Team. A collaboration between our Police Department and Human Services. The Council appropriated $150,000 for Keep Fremont Housed, helping additional families receive up to six months of rental assistance before they lose their homes. We adopted the Emergency Shelter Declaration, expanding our ability to quickly establish emergency housing for those experiencing homelessness. This declaration helped facilitate the opening of Natalie’s Place, 150 units of new interim housing funded through Measure W, a voter‑approved Alameda County initiative. And earlier today we launched a new Homelessness Response Data Dashboard so everyone can see, in real time, how we're responding and the impact our efforts are having. The point's not just that we cleared sites. The point is that we are building a more transparent, disciplined, compassionate, and accountable system. This is the harder work. It doesn’t make headlines or get completed overnight. But we're doing it every single day. And we'll keep doing it with more coordination, transparency, and regional support. Public safety is next — because none of these efforts matter if you don't feel safe in your own neighborhood. In 2025, crime in Fremont fell. Violent crime decreased approximately 13%, and property crime declined roughly 21%. That's not luck. That's a department doing the work. A year ago, we had 40 open police officer vacancies. Today, that number is 17. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont We've closed nearly two-thirds of the gap in less than two years. And 95% of all 9-1-1 calls are answered in 20 seconds or less. Twenty seconds. When you call, we answer. In April, Fremont Police opened the Real-Time Information Center, giving our officers better information, faster coordination, and smarter deployment of resources. In just five months, the center supported more than 250 organized retail theft-related calls, helping protect local businesses and residents. We've strengthened staffing, brought more tools to officers in the field, and heavily invested in training. In particular, our SWAT Team trains and operates in accordance with Tier 1 standards established by the National Tactical Officers Association, the highest professional benchmark for law enforcement tactical teams. And the department is approaching its final steps for CALEA national accreditation. Next month, in July, the Police Department and our City Manager will testify before the commission to receive the accreditation. This demonstrates our commitment to professionalism, accountability, and national best practices. Safety's more than just enforcement, it’s a relationship. Our officers also showed up at more than 20 community events this year. Public safety also expands to our animal residents, who are served by the Tri-City Animal Shelter. This year, the shelter added new volunteers, expanded adoption hours, improved licensing, Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont strengthened social media outreach, funded contract veterinary support, and continued trap-neuter-return work for community cats. As a veterinarian, this work is especially meaningful to me. Animal services are part of how we care for families, protect public health, and serve vulnerable animals in our community. Now, let's talk about our Fremont Fire Department, our team answered more than 19,000 calls. The new truck company in Centerville responded to more than 1,200 emergencies in its first year, improving response in Downtown and Centerville, and supporting growth in South and East Fremont. Fremont Fire completed our first-ever annual inspection of every fire hydrant in the city — more than 5,000 hydrants — and provided more than 147,000 hours of training to personnel. The Department also strengthened emergency medical response, fire prevention, and community safety education through a variety of activities. This includes training more than 40 new Community Emergency Response Team volunteers, holding 2 CERT Basic Training academies, and bringing volunteers together for a citywide drill. All this work is building toward our bigger goal of an ISO Class 1 rating — the highest fire-protection rating a department can earn. Fremont Fire is currently an ISO-2 department, but is going through the reclassification evaluation to continue its efforts to be the greatest resource for the community. Now, preparedness is not just a government function; it’s a community responsibility. And to everybody who keeps this city safe — sworn and civilian, police and fire, dispatchers, animal services, emergency volunteers, and support staff — thank you. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont You're the reason these numbers move. This sense of care expands beyond Public Safety to our other Departments. This year, our Age Well Centers kept thousands of Fremont seniors connected with meals, classes, community, and a place to belong. Our SparkPoint center gave families financial coaching to climb out of debt and start building savings — real steppingstones out of hard times. We invested in youth programs, recreation scholarships, libraries, and the human services that catch people before they fall. Because a city isn’t defined only by how high it builds, but by how well its work serves the next generation. With this, I wanted to share a word about your money. For the 29th consecutive year, our City of Fremont received the Government Finance Officers Association Distinguished Budget Presentation Award. That reflects a long tradition of responsible budgeting and professional financial management. This year, we rebalanced the budget without laying off a single employee, even as personnel costs rose. We were honest about headwinds. High mortgage rates are expected to dampen property-tax revenue through the end of 2026. We know it. We planned for it. That's why prudence matters. The City’s share of the 1% property tax, our largest source of revenue, is determined under State law by our historical share of property tax before Proposition 13 passed in 1978. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont Because Fremont was a low-tax city back then, we’re now locked into a much lower share of property tax than many of our neighboring cities. As a result, despite relatively high property values, we’re challenged to provide the high level of services our community deserves. Even so, we continuously look for ways to do more with less while exercising financial discipline. We’ve utilized our resources, securing one-time funding from federal, state, and county partners — including $850,000 in federal funding for the Auto Mall Parkway Median Project, now 65% of the project design complete — and county funding to support our Age Well Center, SparkPoint’s financial coaching, and Winter Relief. Thank you to our federal, state, county, and regional partners, and to our thoughtful staff for helping Fremont compete for the resources our residents deserve. Now let’s talk about the Fremont you actually live in. For seven years running, WalletHub has named Fremont the Happiest City in America. We've also been recognized as one of the best places to raise a family. Rankings alone do not solve affordability, traffic, or homelessness. But they do reflect something real: people value the quality of life Fremont offers. This year, we broke ground on Phases One and Two of the Central Park Community Center — a long-promised civic anchor that will open in 2028. I am going to say something I don't usually let myself say from this podium: that one's personal. A civic anchor that residents have talked about for years finally started rising on our watch. Beyond that, last summer Aqua Adventure welcomed 58,000 visitors, and 9,300 kids joined our summer camps. We’re looking to grow even more this summer. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont We awarded over 1500 scholarships, helping ensure recreation access for families across our community. Vallejo Mill Community Park has re-opened with new pathways, four pickleball courts, and Fremont’s second dog park nestled in a beautiful natural setting. At Central Park, we replaced the Dog park turf, which is just a short walk from the new shaded outdoor exercise equipment. At Azevada Park, the play equipment was also replaced with new structures. For a quieter experience, visit our beautiful new entry rose garden at California Nursery Historical Park. It's a stunning addition to the park, and soon to be available to host weddings and your most elegant events, made possible thanks to the generous donations from our very own Fremont Residents Nalini and Hemant Gupta and Fremont Bank. We made many improvements in our park system. Including 26 new drinking fountains with bottle fillers at Central Park, and the work continues. With the modernization of an additional 18 aging park restroom buildings to make them ADA-compliant and equipped with babychanging stations. These may sound like small details. But any parent, senior, coach, athlete, or family spending the day at a park knows how much they matter. Speaking of parks, we also launched the Lake Elizabeth Water Quality Improvement Pilot Project to protect wildlife, stabilize water temperatures, and maintain healthy oxygen levels in the lake. And this year, we brought pedal boating back to a portion of the lake. For many families, that's not just recreation. It's nostalgia, memory, and community returning to one of Fremont’s most beloved places. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont But it's not only parks. Our libraries, our public art, and our cultural festivals — Lunar New Year, Diwali, Holidays at the Plaza, Pride celebrations, and the many community events that fill our calendar — are part of what makes Fremont one of the most diverse and welcoming cities in America. Walk through a Fremont festival on a Saturday and you'll hear a dozen languages, smell food from every corner of the world, and see neighbors who came here from everywhere building one community together. We celebrate our differences here, and that’s what makes our community special. That, too, is Fremont, and it's helping our Downtown come alive. And this year, I had the privilege of cutting the ribbon at Pour Decisions — a bar and café opening its third location and its first in Alameda County, right here in Downtown Fremont. We welcomed Pizza My Heart in Downtown Fremont as well as Palmetto Superfoods, Stardust Coffee House, and other businesses that are helping bring life to the heart of the city. These small businesses choosing Fremont is the most honest review of our Downtown. Every new café, every new shop, and every lit-up storefront on a Downtown evening is a family betting its savings on this city. Our job is to make sure that bet pays off. This year, we worked to streamline permitting and make City Hall more responsive, practical, and focused on helping good businesses open faster. Every week, we save a small-business owner is a week of payroll, rent, and a dream not deferred. We owe them a City Hall that moves with urgency, and we're working to deliver it. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont We also owe them a true community, and our events help to foster this sense of belonging. Summer Concerts at Central Park. Movie Nights in the Parks. Holidays at the Plaza. Street Eats out front, like I told you about. If you ask me what my favorite thing about being Mayor of Fremont is, honestly, it's one of those nights. Three generations of one family, sharing a meal while a band plays. Strangers who've never met suddenly realizing they're neighbors. That right there is what every single one of those manufacturing leases I talked about earlier this evening is for. That evening at Street Eats — talking with Kathy in the plaza, watching the city she's lived in for more than 50 years come alive around us — that's the Fremont we're building. That's the Fremont we're protecting. With that, I wanted to share a quick update on sustainability. Fremont has been a Tree City USA for 29 years and planted 1,540 trees throughout the city in 2025, making us a top-ranked green city. Over the past year, we installed solar and battery-storage microgrids at the Age Well Center in South Fremont and Tri-City Volunteers Food Bank and Mobile Pantry. We also extended our recycling processing agreement with BLT Enterprises to help support a $10 million dollar high-tech transformation of the Fremont Recycling and Transfer Station and are expanding our City fleet with more EVs and charging stations. After transitioning residential customers to 100% renewable energy through Ava Community Energy, commercial customers are next, moving to Renewable 100 in August. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont For us, sustainability's not about slogans. It's about resilience, lower emissions, cleaner infrastructure, and practical improvements residents can feel. Regarding transportation, the Irvington BART Station continues to be a focus, named by Plan Bay Area 2050 as a near-term priority. Our environmental clearances are complete, 10 housing developments have already been built in anticipation of this station, and we have a third of the construction money in hand. We need the rest. Fighting for the funding to finish Irvington BART is one of our top priorities in the years ahead. We'll not let this slip. Beyond these marquee projects, this year we made traffic safety a priority. We’ve increased enforcement to ensure safer driving behavior, expanding the use of red-light cameras, and bringing back our dedicated Traffic Unit to focus on high-risk areas. Our early efforts have resulted in an increase of 137% of written citations. While Fremont’s fatal crash rate is below the national average, every life matters — and we're committed to doing everything we can to protect them. Unfortunately this past weekend's incident reinforces our commitment to traffic safety. To reduce risks, we’re installing eight new flashing pedestrian beacons and adding seven grant-funded speed alert message board trailers for our roadways. We also modernized traffic signals across the city, repaired more than 1,300 potholes, completed more than 1,200 sidewalk repairs, processed approximately 1,700 public maintenance requests, and kept building safer routes for people who walk and bike every day. A future-ready city must also be a Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont well-maintained city. We're focused on both. Part of having a well-maintained city is having a government that works. And one of my aims is that residents who don't understand City Hall, can still get the help they need from City Hall. This means making City services easier to find, use, and trust. This year, we launched Access Fremont, our free public Wi-Fi network, with 125 access points across six business districts and the Ohlone College area. This enhancement closes the digital divide, supports small businesses, and gives residents another way to stay connected. To support this initiative further, we won federal grant funding to bring high-speed fiber to 514 locations in our city that had been left behind, and we're upgrading City websites and digital services to improve accessibility, clarity, and ease of use — especially for residents with disabilities — and we improved cell coverage at City facilities. Behind the scenes, we also modernized the systems our own crews use, so the people who fix your streets and maintain your parks can do more, faster. As a result, our Fleet team completed 10% more work orders. We want to make it easier to get services from your city every single year. And this year, we accomplished this goal. Now I don’t think you can get through a speech in 2026 and not talk about AI. We're also looking at ways to responsibly use AI tools to help residents find information faster, improve internal efficiency, and support better customer service — while keeping privacy, accuracy, Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont and accountability central. Beyond our city limits... Remember those relationships I told you I spent year one building? This is where they show up. Today, I have the honor of serving as President of the East Bay Division of the League of California Cities, representing Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, Vice President of the Alameda County Mayors’ Conference, and I joined Climate Mayors. Those aren't honorary titles. They're seats at the table — on climate, housing, transportation, infrastructure, homelessness, and local control — where the decisions that shape our region get made. A city this size, with this story, has earned the right to help set that agenda. And when Fremont speaks, the region listens. Now, none of what I have described tonight happens without the incredible City employees who show up every day to serve our neighbors. This includes crews who fill the potholes, planners who keep us building, dispatchers who answer in twenty seconds, and the librarians, lifeguards, social workers, engineers, maintenance workers, firefighters, police officers, animal shelter staff, records clerks, recreation leaders, customer service staff, and countless others who dedicate their late nights and early mornings to this incredibly hard yet rewarding work. Thank you for being the unsung heroes behind this monumental progress. Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont Your combined efforts are helping Fremont reach never-before-seen heights. Of course, all this happens also because of you — the residents — who serve on our boards and commissions, volunteer at our events, coach teams, clean up creeks, support schools, mentor youth, run businesses, and show up to public comment after work when you’re tired because you love this place. Fremont works because Fremonters do the work. We want to thank you. I’d be remised if I didn’t take this moment to also give a special thank-you to outgoing Public Works Director Hans Larsen and Police Chief Sean Washington for their years of service to Fremont. Congratulations are also in order for Joel Pullen, on his promotion to Community Development Director; our new Police Chief, Floyd Mitchell; and we also welcome Matt Cano, our new Public Works Director. To their families and to every family that shares a public servant with this city, thank you. In July, the City Council will consider a proposed Charter City measure and whether to place it before Fremont voters. Please get involved. Information will be available through the City Clerk’s office and the City’s website. And if you want more updates on how our City initiatives are progressing, I strongly recommend subscribing to our community newsletters. They provide updates about all the happenings in Fremont from ongoing measures to new hires and events, such as our upcoming Fourth of July festivities, including the return of our beloved Fourth of July Parade, and remember to check out our first-ever drone show, this Thursday, July 2nd, Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont to celebrate America’s 250th, at Central Park. To wrap up, I want to come back to that evening at Street Eats. To Kathy — sitting with me in the plaza — talking about what she wanted for her grandkids. Because that's the whole point of this job. Seventy years ago, the people of Centerville, Mission San José, Niles, Irvington, and Warm Springs took a chance on each other. This year, we didn't just keep that chance alive; we doubled down on it. Now check out our Sizzle Reel that highlights our accomplishments from the past year. < Sizzle Reel plays in background as Mayor speaks> We became the manufacturing capital of an entire region, delivered hundreds of affordable homes, brought crime down, strengthened public safety staffing and technology, and responded to homelessness with more transparency, services, and accountability. We also brought new life to Downtown with expanded digital access, protected parks, invested in Lake Elizabeth, and started building a community center our grandchildren will grow up in. Fremont hit its stride. But none of that's the point. The point is, the family on the blanket, the child splashing through Aqua Adventure on a Tuesday, the senior walking into the Age Well Center and finding community, Mayor Salwan, City of Fremont and the small-business owner who chose to open a Downtown location because they believed in what we're building here. The point is, the student who walks into a manufacturing facility and sees a future career in the city where they grew up. Our aim is to ensure every single Fremont resident can feel that the future is being built for them. Next year, the Community Center comes out of the ground.
